    About notations

    In this section, we fix some notations and normalizations to avoid misleading. When we have to use different conventions, we give an explanation.

    Wegde products

    Edit

    Following John M Lee's book, we define

    \begin{equation*} \text { Alt } \alpha=\frac{1}{k !} \sum_{\sigma \in S_{k}}(\operatorname{sgn} \sigma)\left({ }^{\sigma} \alpha\right), \text { Sym } \alpha=\frac{1}{k !} \sum_{\sigma \in S_{k}}{ }^{\sigma} \alpha, \end{equation*}

    and

    \begin{equation*} \omega \wedge \eta=\frac{(k+l) !}{k ! l !} \operatorname{Alt}(\omega \otimes \eta), \quad \alpha \beta= \operatorname{Sym}(\alpha \otimes \beta). \end{equation*}

    Then one can show that

    \begin{equation} \Phi \wedge\Psi \wedge \eta=\frac{(r+s+t) !}{r ! s ! t !} \operatorname{Alt}(\Phi \otimes \Psi \otimes \eta). \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} \omega^{i_{1}} \wedge \omega^{i_{2}} \wedge \cdots \wedge \omega^{i_{r}}=r ! \operatorname{Alt}\left(\omega^{i_{1}} \otimes \omega^{i_{2}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \omega^{i_{r}}\right). \end{equation}

    The interior product and the exterior product are

    Lemma
    Edit

    Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and \(v\in V\).

    1. \[ i_v\circ i_v=0. \]

    2. If \(\omega\in\Lambda^k(V^*)\) and \(\eta\in\Lambda^l(V^*)\), then

      \[ i_v(\omega\wedge\eta) = (i_v\omega)\wedge\eta + (-1)^k\omega\wedge(i_v\eta). \]

    Theorem
    Edit


    Suppose \(M\) is a smooth manifold with or without boundary. There are unique operators

    \[ d:\Omega^k(M)\to \Omega^{k+1}(M) \]

    for all \(k\), called exterior differentiation, satisfying the following four properties:

    1. \(d\) is linear over \(\mathbb{R}\).

    2. If \(\omega\in\Omega^k(M)\) and \(\eta\in\Omega^l(M)\), then

      \[ d(\omega\wedge\eta) = d\omega\wedge\eta + (-1)^k\omega\wedge d\eta. \]

    3. \[ d\circ d\equiv 0. \]

    4. For \(f\in\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)\), \(df\) is the differential of \(f\), given by

      \[ df(X)=Xf. \]

    Remark
    Edit

    Compare with alt convention \(\bar\wedge, \bar d\) of Kobayashi-Nomizu's book:

    \begin{equation*} \eta_{(k)} \bar \wedge \omega_{(l)} =\operatorname{Alt}(\omega \otimes \eta), \quad \eta \bar \wedge \omega =\frac{k!l!}{(k+l)!} \eta \wedge \omega, \quad \bar d \eta =\frac{1}{k+1} d \eta, \end{equation*}

    and

    \begin{equation} \omega^{i_{1}} \wedge \omega^{i_{2}} \wedge \cdots \wedge \omega^{i_{r}}=r ! \omega^{i_{1}}\bar \wedge \omega^{i_{2}} \bar \wedge \cdots \bar \wedge \omega^{i_{r}}. \end{equation}

    The Alt convention is more common in complex differential geometry.

    When the wedge product is defined using the Alt convention, interior multiplication of a vector with a \(k\)-form has to be defined with an extra factor of \(k\):

    \[ \bar{\iota}_v\omega(w_1,\ldots,w_{k-1}) = k\,\omega(v,w_1,\ldots,w_{k-1}), \]

    and the exterior differentiation is

    \[ \bar{d} \omega = \frac{1}{k+1} d \omega . \]

    Under these conventions, the formulas in Lemma ?? and Theorem ?? are still valid.

    Curvatures

    Edit

    Christoffel symbols

    Edit

    Let \(\nabla \) be Levi-Civita connection. Set

    \[\nabla_{\frac{\partial }{\partial x^i}} \frac{\partial }{\partial x^j} := \Gamma_{i j}^{k} \frac{\partial }{\partial x^k},\]

    then

    \begin{equation} \boxed{\Gamma_{i j}^{k}=\frac{1}{2} g^{k \ell}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i}} g_{j \ell}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}} g_{i \ell}-\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\ell}} g_{i j}\right).} \end{equation}

    Change of coordinates:

    \begin{equation*} \Gamma_{i j}^{k}=\tilde{\Gamma}_{p q}^{r} \frac{\partial \tilde{x}^{p}}{\partial x^{i}} \frac{\partial \tilde{x}^{q}}{\partial x^{j}} \frac{\partial x^{k}}{\partial \tilde{x}^{r}}+\frac{\partial^{2} \tilde{x}^{r}}{\partial x^{i} \partial x^{j}} \frac{\partial x^{k}}{\partial \tilde{x}^{r}}. \end{equation*}

    \begin{equation*} g_{i j}=\tilde{g}_{p q} \frac{\partial \tilde{x}^{p}}{\partial x^{i}} \frac{\partial \tilde{x}^{q}}{\partial x^{j}}. \end{equation*}

    When using moving frame, given \(\tilde{E}_{i}=A_{i}^{j} E_{j}\), then

    \begin{equation*} \tilde{\Gamma}_{i j}^{k}=\left(A^{-1}\right)_{p}^{k} A_{i}^{q} A_{j}^{r} \Gamma_{q r}^{p}+\left(A^{-1}\right)_{p}^{k} A_{i}^{q} E_{q}\left(A_{j}^{p}\right). \end{equation*}

    Let \(\varphi:N\to M\) be a immersion, then

    \begin{equation*} \Gamma\left(\varphi^{*} g\right)_{\alpha \beta}^{\gamma} \frac{\partial \varphi^{k}}{\partial y^{\gamma}}=\left(\Gamma_{i j}^{k} \circ \varphi\right) \frac{\partial \varphi^{i}}{\partial y^{\alpha}} \frac{\partial \varphi^{j}}{\partial y^{\beta}}+\frac{\partial^{2} \varphi^{k}}{\partial y^{\alpha} \partial y^{\beta}}. \end{equation*}

    In moving frames:

    \begin{equation*} \Gamma_{k j}^i=\omega^i\left(\nabla_{e_k} e_j\right)=\omega_j^i\left(e_k\right) . \end{equation*}

    Change of frames: \(\bar{e}_i=a_i^ke_k,\) and \((b_i^j)\) inverts \((a_i^j)\) (thus \(\bar{\omega}^i=b^i_j \omega^j\), \(b_k^j a^k_i=\delta_{ij}\) and \(b_j^k a^i_k=\delta_{ij}\)), then

    \begin{equation} \overline{\omega_j^i}=\left(a_j^l \omega_l^k+d a_j^k\right) b_k^i . \end{equation}

    Riemannian Curvature tensor

    Edit

    We adopt the following convention:

    \begin{equation} \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &R(X, Y) Z=\nabla_{X} \nabla_{Y} Z-\nabla_{Y} \nabla_{X} Z-\nabla_{[X, Y]} Z,\\ &R(X, Y, Z, W)=\langle R(Z,W) Y, X\rangle. \end{aligned}} \end{equation}

    Local coefficients are

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &R(e_k,e_l)e_j=R_{jkl}^h e_h,\\ &R_{ijkl}=R(e_i,e_j,e_k,e_l)=g_{ih}R_{jkl}^h. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    Torsion tensor:

    \begin{equation*} T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY -\nabla_YX-[X,Y]. \end{equation*}

    Remark
    Edit

    Sectional, Ricci, scalar curvature:

    \[ \begin{aligned} &K(u, v)=\frac{R(u, v, u, v)}{\|u \wedge v\|^{2}}, \\ & \ricci(X, Y)=\trace(Z \rightarrow R(Z,X) Y)=\la R(e_i,X)Y,e_i \ra=R(X,e_i,Y,e_i),\\ &\sc=\trace \ricci=R_{i}^{i}=g^{i j} R_{i j}. \end{aligned} \]

    Note that for a linear transformation \(A=(a_{j}^{i})\),

    \[ \begin{pmatrix} \widetilde u\\ \widetilde v \end{pmatrix} =A\begin{pmatrix} u\\ v \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1^1&a_2^1\\ a_1^2&a_2^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u\\ v \end{pmatrix}. \]

    we have

    \begin{equation*} \|\tilde{u} \wedge \tilde{v}\|^{2}=\left( \operatorname{det}\left(A\right)\right)^{2}\|u \wedge v\|^{2},\quad R(\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}, \tilde{u}, \tilde{v})=\left(\operatorname{det} \left(A\right)\right)^{2} R(u, v, u, v). \end{equation*}

    Proposition
    Edit

    For Levi-Civita connection, we have the following curvature symmetries:

    \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \text { (i) } R(X, Y) Z+R(Y, X) Z=0, \\ & \text { (ii) } R(X, Y) Z+R(Y, Z) X+R(Z, X) Y=0, \\ & \text { (iii) } R(X, Y, Z, W)=-R(Y, X, Z, W) =-R(X, Y, W, Z), \\ & \text { (iv) } R(X, Y, Z, W)=R(Z, W, X, Y) , \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

    or

    \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} \text { (i) } R_{j k l}^i+R_{j l k}^i=0, \\ \text { (ii) } R_{j k l}^i+R_{k l j}^i+R_{i j k}^i=0, \\ \qquad R_{i j k l}+R_{i k l j}+R_{i j k k}=0, \\ \text { (iii) } R_{i j k l}=-R_{j i k l}=-R_{i j k l}, \\ \text { (iv) } R_{i j k l}=R_{k l i j} . \end{array}\right. \end{equation}

    Moreover, the Second Bianchi identity holds:

    \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \nabla R(V, W, X, Y ; Z)+\nabla R(V, W, Y, Z ; X)+ \nabla R(V, W, Z, X ; Y)=0, \end{gathered} \end{equation}

    or

    \begin{equation} R_{ijkl,h}+R_{ijlh,k}+R_{ijhk,l}=0. \end{equation}

    In a local coordinate, we have

    \[ \begin{aligned} R_{j k l}^i & =\Omega_j^i\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l}\right) \\ & =\boxed{\frac{\partial \Gamma_{l j}^i}{\partial x^k}-\frac{\partial \Gamma_{k j}^i}{\partial x^l}+\Gamma_{l j}^h \Gamma_{k h}^i-\Gamma_{k j}^h \Gamma_{l h}^i} . \end{aligned} \]

    Covariant derivatives

    Edit

    Write an \((r,s)\)-type tensor \(\phi \in T_{s}^{r}(M)\) as

    \begin{equation} \phi=\phi_{j_1 \cdots j_i}^{i_i \cdots i_s} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_r}} \otimes d x^{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes d x^{j_s}. \end{equation}

    Given a linear connection \(\nabla \), we wrtie the covariant derivate of \(\phi \) as

    \begin{equation} \nabla_X \phi=X^k \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s,k}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_r}} \otimes d x^{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes d x^{j_s}. \end{equation}

    Hence

    \begin{equation} \phi_{j_{1} \cdots j_{s, k}}^{i_{1} \cdots i_{r}}= \frac{\partial \phi_{j_{1} \cdots j_{s}}^{i_{1} \cdots i_{r}}}{\partial x^{k}}+\sum_{t=1}^{r} \Gamma_{kl}^{i_{t}} \phi_{j_{1} \cdots j_{s}}^{i_{1} \cdots i_{t-1} l i_{t+1} \cdots i_{r}}- \sum_{t=1}^{s} \Gamma_{k j_{t}}^{l} \phi_{j_{1} \cdots j_{t-1}l j_{t+1} \cdots j_{s}}^{i_{1} \cdots i_{r}}, \end{equation}

    \begin{equation} \nabla \phi=\phi_{j_1 \cdots j_j, k}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} d x^k \otimes \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_r}} \otimes d x^{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes d x^{j_1}. \end{equation}

    Second derivative for a tensor \(\phi:\)

    \begin{equation} \nabla^2 \phi(\cdots ; X, Y)=\left(\nabla_Y\left(\nabla_X \phi\right)\right)(\cdots)-\nabla_{\nabla_Y X} \phi(\cdots). \end{equation}

    Proposition (Ricci identity)
    Edit

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \nabla^2 \phi(\cdots ; X, Y)-\nabla^2 \phi(\cdots ; Y, X) \\ = & R(Y, X) \phi(\cdots)=-R(X, Y) \phi(\cdots) , \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    under frames:

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s, k l}^{i_1 \cdots i_r}-\phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s, l k}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} \\ = & \sum_{\alpha=1}^s \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_{\alpha-1} h j_{\alpha+1} \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} R_{j_\alpha k l}^h- \sum_{\beta=1}^r \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_{\beta-1} h i_{\beta+1} \cdots i_r} R_{h k l}^{i_\beta} . \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    Set

    \begin{equation} \nabla_X e_i=\omega_i^j(X) e_j, \quad \nabla_X \omega^i=-\omega_j^i(X) \omega^j, \end{equation}

    thus the Christoffel symbols are given by

    \[ \Gamma _{ji}^{k}= \omega _{i}^{k}(e_{j}). \]

    Define

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & D \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} :=\phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s, k}^{i_1 \cdots i_r} \omega^k=d \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_r}+\sum_{t=1}^{r} \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_{t-1} l i_{t+1} \cdots i_r} \omega_l^{i_t}- \sum_{t=1}^s \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_{t-1} l j_{t+1} \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_{r}} \omega^l_{j_t}, \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    then

    \begin{equation} \nabla \phi=\left(D \phi_{j_1 \cdots j_s}^{i_1 \cdots i_r}\right) \otimes e_{i_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes e_{i_1} \otimes \omega^{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \omega^{j_s}. \end{equation}

    Connection forms

    Edit

    Let

    \begin{gather*} T(X,Y)=T^i(X,Y)e_i\\ R(X,Y)e_i=\Omega^j_i(X,Y)e_j \end{gather*}

    Proposition (Cartan structure equations)
    Edit

    \begin{gather*} d \omega^i=-\omega^i_k \wedge \omega^k+T^i\\ d \omega_j^i=-\omega^i_k \wedge \omega^k_j+\Omega^i_j. \end{gather*}

    In particular, when \(\{e_i\}\) is orthonormal and the connection \(\nabla\) is metric, we have

    \begin{equation*} \omega^i_j+\omega^j_i=0. \end{equation*}

    Let

    \begin{equation*} T^i=\frac{1}{2} T_{j k}^i \omega^j \wedge \omega^k, \quad T_{j k}^i=-T_{k j}^i, \end{equation*}

    \begin{equation*} \Omega_j^i=\frac{1}{2} R_{j k l}^i \omega^k \wedge \omega^l, \quad R_{j k l}^i=-R_{j l k}^i. \end{equation*}

    Proposition
    Edit

    For a linear connection under a coordinate, we have

    \begin{align*} T_{j k}^i &=\Gamma_{j k}^i-\Gamma_{k j}^i \\ R_{j k l}^i & =\Omega_j^i\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l}\right) \\ & =\frac{\partial \Gamma_{l j}^i}{\partial x^k}-\frac{\partial \Gamma_{k j}^i}{\partial x^l}+\Gamma_{l j}^h \Gamma_{k h}^i-\Gamma_{k j}^h \Gamma_{l h}^i. \end{align*}

    Remark
    Edit

    On an almost complex manifold \(M^{2n}\), we set

    \[\varphi^\alpha =\omega ^\alpha +i \omega ^{n+\alpha} , \quad \psi^\alpha _\beta=\omega ^\alpha _\beta +i \omega ^\alpha _{n+\beta}, \quad \alpha ,\beta =1,...,n ;\]

    \[ \Phi^\alpha =T^\alpha +i T^{n+\alpha },\quad \Psi^{\alpha }_\beta=\Omega ^\alpha _\beta +i \Omega ^\alpha _{n+\beta}, \quad \alpha ,\beta =1,...,n ;\]

    then

    \begin{gather*} d \varphi^\alpha=-\psi^\alpha _\beta \wedge \varphi^\beta+\Phi^\alpha\\ d \psi^\alpha _\beta=-\psi^\alpha _\gamma \wedge \psi^\gamma_\beta+\Psi^{\alpha }_\beta. \end{gather*}

    Set

    \[ z_{\alpha }=\frac{1}{2}(e_\alpha -iJe_{\alpha }), \]

    and denote \(Je_\alpha =e_{n+\alpha }\), then \(\{z_\alpha \}\) is the dual of \(\{\varphi^\alpha \}\). When \(M\) is Kählerian, see Kaeh.

    Example (Pull-backs)
    Edit

    Let \(y=y(x): M\to N\) be a smooth map. Let \(dy=y_\alpha^i dx^{\alpha}\otimes \frac{\partial }{\partial y^i},\nabla dy=y_{\alpha \beta}^i dx^{\beta}\otimes dx^{\alpha}\otimes \frac{\partial }{\partial y^i}\). Then

    \begin{equation*} y_\alpha^i=\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^\alpha} ; \quad y_{\alpha \beta}^i=\frac{\partial^2 y^i}{\partial x^\alpha \partial x^\beta}- ^M\Gamma_{\alpha \beta}^\gamma y_\gamma^i+ ^N\Gamma_{j k}^i y_\alpha^j y_{\beta}^k. \end{equation*}

    Similarly,

    \begin{equation} \boxed{ f_{i j k}^I-f_{i k j}^I=f_l^I R_{ijk}^l-f_i^J f_j^K f_k^L \tilde{R}_{J K L}^I.} \end{equation}
